34.0.1 Question 1
In the elastic net objective \[
\frac{1}{2N}\|y-Xw\|_2^2+\lambda\left(\rho\|w\|_1+\frac{1-\rho}{2}\|w\|_2^2\right),
\] state the role of \(\lambda\) and the role of \(\rho\). What happens at \(\rho=0\) and \(\rho=1\)?


Answer

The parameter \(\lambda\ge0\) controls the overall strength of regularization. Larger \(\lambda\) places more weight on the penalty relative to the squared-error fit term.
The parameter \(\rho\in[0,1]\) controls the mix between the \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_2\) parts. At \(\rho=1\), the penalty is purely \(\ell_1\), giving LASSO. At \(\rho=0\), the penalty is purely squared \(\ell_2\), giving ridge up to constant scaling of \(\lambda\).



34.0.2 Question 2
For \(w=(2,-1,0)\), \(\lambda=3\), and \(\rho=0.4\), compute the elastic net penalty term \[
\lambda\left(\rho\|w\|_1+\frac{1-\rho}{2}\|w\|_2^2\right).
\]


Answer

First, \[
\|w\|_1=|2|+|-1|+0=3,
\] and \[
\|w\|_2^2=2^2+(-1)^2+0^2=5.
\] Thus the unscaled mixed penalty is \[
0.4(3)+\frac{1-0.4}{2}(5)=1.2+0.3(5)=1.2+1.5=2.7.
\] Multiplying by \(\lambda=3\) gives \[
3(2.7)=8.1.
\]



34.0.3 Question 3
Why does the lecture say elastic net is especially useful when predictors are strongly correlated? Compare the expected coefficient behavior of ridge, LASSO, and elastic net in a correlated signal group.


Answer

Ridge tends to spread weight across correlated predictors because its \(\ell_2\) penalty stabilizes large coefficient swings but does not create exact zeros. LASSO encourages sparsity, so in a correlated group it may select one representative variable and set the others to zero, which can make selected variables unstable.
Elastic net combines these behaviors. Its \(\ell_1\) part can remove irrelevant variables, while its \(\ell_2\) part encourages stability and can keep several variables from a correlated signal group instead of forcing a single representative.



34.0.4 Question 4
The lecture’s coordinate update is \[
w_j\leftarrow \frac{S(z_j,\lambda\rho)}{a_j+\lambda(1-\rho)}.
\] Show explicitly that this reduces to the LASSO update when \(\rho=1\) and to a ridge-like update when \(\rho=0\).


Answer

If \(\rho=1\), then the threshold is \(\lambda\rho=\lambda\) and the denominator is \[
a_j+\lambda(1-1)=a_j.
\] Thus \[
w_j\leftarrow \frac{S(z_j,\lambda)}{a_j},
\] which is the LASSO coordinate update.
If \(\rho=0\), then the threshold is \(0\), so \(S(z_j,0)=z_j\), and the denominator is \[
a_j+\lambda.
\] Thus \[
w_j\leftarrow \frac{z_j}{a_j+\lambda},
\] which is ridge-like shrinkage.



34.0.5 Question 5
For intermediate \(0<\rho<1\), why does elastic net both threshold and shrink? Use the coordinate update formula in your answer.


Answer

The numerator \[
S(z_j,\lambda\rho)
\] soft-thresholds \(z_j\). If \(|z_j|\le\lambda\rho\), the numerator is zero, so the coefficient is set exactly to zero. This is the LASSO-like thresholding effect.
When \(|z_j|>\lambda\rho\), the numerator is nonzero but has reduced magnitude. Then the denominator \[
a_j+\lambda(1-\rho)
\] further shrinks the coefficient. This is the ridge-like stabilization effect.



34.0.6 Question 6
Assume standardized predictors so \(a_j=1\). Let \(z_j=2.5\), \(\lambda=1\), and \(\rho=0.5\). Compute the elastic net coordinate update.


Answer

The threshold is \[
\lambda\rho=1(0.5)=0.5.
\] Since \(z_j=2.5>0.5\), \[
S(2.5,0.5)=2.5-0.5=2.0.
\] The denominator is \[
a_j+\lambda(1-\rho)=1+1(0.5)=1.5.
\] Thus \[
w_j\leftarrow \frac{2.0}{1.5}=\frac43.
\]



34.0.7 Question 7
Suppose \(z_j=0.3\), \(a_j=1\), \(\lambda=1\), and \(\rho=0.5\). Compute the elastic net coordinate update.


Answer

The threshold is \[
\lambda\rho=0.5.
\] Since \(|z_j|=0.3\le0.5\), \[
S(z_j,0.5)=0.
\] Therefore \[
w_j\leftarrow \frac{0}{1+1(1-0.5)}=0.
\] The coordinate signal is not strong enough to overcome the \(\ell_1\) part of the penalty, so the coefficient is set to zero.



34.0.8 Question 8
The lecture says different books and software use different constants in front of the squared-error and ridge terms. Explain why multiplying the whole penalty by a constant often only changes the scale of \(\lambda\) rather than the statistical idea.


Answer

Suppose an objective contains \[
\lambda c\,\Omega(w)
\] for some positive constant \(c\). If we define a new tuning parameter \[
\lambda'=c\lambda,
\] then the penalty becomes \[
\lambda'\Omega(w).
\] Thus changing constants can often be absorbed by changing the numerical value of \(\lambda\). The path is parameterized differently, but the basic fit-complexity tradeoff is the same.



34.0.9 Question 9
Why does tuning elastic net generally require a two-dimensional grid search, while ridge and LASSO each require only a one-dimensional penalty search in the lecture’s setup?


Answer

Ridge and LASSO each have one main penalty-strength parameter, \(\lambda\), after the penalty type is fixed. Elastic net has both the overall strength \(\lambda\) and the mixing parameter \(\rho\).
The value of \(\lambda\) controls how much regularization is applied, while \(\rho\) controls the balance between \(\ell_1\) sparsity and \(\ell_2\) stabilization. Both affect the fitted model, so cross-validation typically searches over pairs \((\lambda,\rho)\).



34.0.10 Question 10
Why is the intercept \(w_0\) usually not penalized in penalized logistic regression, according to the same logic used for ridge and LASSO?


Answer

The intercept controls the baseline log-odds, or baseline class probability, before feature effects are applied. It is not a measure of model complexity in the same way that feature coefficients are.
Penalizing \(w_0\) would artificially shrink the baseline probability toward a default value, potentially introducing unnecessary bias. Therefore the penalty is usually applied only to \(w\), not to \(w_0\).



34.0.11 Question 11
In sklearn, suppose two logistic models differ only in C: one has C=0.01 and one has C=100. Which one is more strongly regularized? Which one would you expect to have more nonzero coefficients under an elastic net penalty with fixed l1_ratio?


Answer

C is inverse regularization strength, so smaller C means stronger regularization. Thus C=0.01 is more strongly regularized than C=100.
With fixed l1_ratio, the model with C=100 has weaker regularization, so more coefficients can enter the model. The model with C=0.01 is expected to have fewer nonzero coefficients.



34.0.12 Question 12
Map the sklearn parameter l1_ratio to the lecture’s penalty mix. What do l1_ratio=0, l1_ratio=1, and l1_ratio=0.5 mean?


Answer

l1_ratio plays the role of the elastic net mixing parameter \(\rho\).

l1_ratio=0 means \(\rho=0\), giving a purely ridge-like logistic penalty.
l1_ratio=1 means \(\rho=1\), giving a purely LASSO logistic penalty.
l1_ratio=0.5 gives an elastic net penalty with both \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_2\) components.




34.0.13 Question 13
For an elastic net logistic path with fixed l1_ratio=0.5, suppose the nonzero counts at \(C=0.01,0.1,1,10\) are \(2,8,18,30\). Interpret the trend in terms of regularization strength.


Answer

As \(C\) increases, regularization weakens because \(C\) is inverse regularization strength. With weaker regularization, more coefficients are allowed to enter the model.
The nonzero counts increasing from \(2\) to \(30\) are therefore consistent with the lecture’s statement that larger \(C\) allows larger and more numerous coefficients.

title: 35  Feed-Forward Neural Networks - Review Questions
text:

35.0.1 Question 1
A network has layer sizes \[
[3,4,3,1].
\] I.e. it has a 3-vector input and outputs a single number. Using the lecture’s formula, compute the number of parameters in each layer and the total number of parameters.


Answer

For a layer mapping width \(d_{i-1}\) to width \(d_i\), the number of parameters is \[
d_id_{i-1}+d_i.
\] For \(3\to4\): \[
4\cdot3+4=16.
\] For \(4\to3\): \[
3\cdot4+3=15.
\] For \(3\to1\): \[
1\cdot3+1=4.
\] The total is \[
16+15+4=35.
\]



35.0.2 Question 3
The lecture contrasts feature engineering and feature learning. What’s the difference?


Answer

Feature engineering manually constructs new inputs before fitting a model. For example, one could replace \(x=(x_1,x_2)\) by \[
(x_1,x_2,x_1^2,x_2^2,x_1x_2)
\] and then fit a linear model in this expanded representation.
Feature learning lets the model learn intermediate features from data. In a neural network, the first hidden layer might compute \[
h^{(1)}=\phi(W^{(1)}x+b^{(1)}),
\] so the learned features are the coordinates of \(h^{(1)}\) rather than manually specified polynomial terms.



35.0.3 Question 2
Suppose layer \(i\) has input dimension \(d_{i-1}=5\) and output dimension \(d_i=7\). State the dimensions of \(W^{(i)}\), \(b^{(i)}\), \(W^{(i)}h+b^{(i)}\), and \(s_i(h)\).


Answer

The weight matrix has shape \[
W^{(i)}\in\mathbb R^{7\times5}.
\] The bias vector has shape \[
b^{(i)}\in\mathbb R^7.
\] For \(h\in\mathbb R^5\), \[
W^{(i)}h\in\mathbb R^7,
\] so \[
W^{(i)}h+b^{(i)}\in\mathbb R^7.
\] Because \(\phi_i\) maps \(\mathbb R^7\) to \(\mathbb R^7\) componentwise, \[
s_i(h)=\phi_i(W^{(i)}h+b^{(i)})\in\mathbb R^7.
\]



35.0.4 Question 3
A one-hidden-layer regression network has input dimension \(D=10\), \(H=6\) hidden units, and a single output dimension. It uses \[
h=\phi(Wx+b),\qquad s_\theta(x)=v^\top h+c.
\] Compute the total number of parameters.


Answer

The hidden layer has \[
W\in\mathbb R^{6\times10}
\] with \(60\) weights and \[
b\in\mathbb R^6
\] with \(6\) biases. That is \(66\) hidden-layer parameters.
The output layer has \[
v\in\mathbb R^6
\] with \(6\) weights and scalar bias \(c\), giving \(7\) output-layer parameters.
The total is \[
66+7=73.
\]



35.0.5 Question 4
Why are nonlinear activation functions essential if we want a multilayer network to represent more than a linear model?


Answer

If every activation is the identity, then each layer is just an affine transformation. A composition of affine transformations is itself affine. Therefore, even a deep network with only identity activations collapses to a single affine score function. Nonlinear activations such as ReLU, sigmoid, or tanh prevent this collapse. They allow the network to build nonlinear transformations of the input and become more flexible than a linear model.



35.0.6 Question 5
Prove that a two-layer network with identity activations is affine. Specifically, let \[
h=W^{(1)}x+b^{(1)},
\qquad
s(x)=W^{(2)}h+b^{(2)}.
\] Write \(s(x)\) as a single affine function of \(x\): \[
s(x)=Ax+a.
\]


Answer

Substitute the first layer into the second: \[
s(x)=W^{(2)}(W^{(1)}x+b^{(1)})+b^{(2)}.
\] Distribute: \[
s(x)=W^{(2)}W^{(1)}x+W^{(2)}b^{(1)}+b^{(2)}.
\] This has the form \[
s(x)=Ax+a,
\] where \[
A=W^{(2)}W^{(1)},
\qquad
a=W^{(2)}b^{(1)}+b^{(2)}.
\] Thus the two-layer identity-activation network is just one affine map.



35.0.7 Question 6
What does it mean for a network to be feed-forward?


Answer

Feed-forward means information moves in one direction through the network. The input \(x\) is transformed into the first hidden representation \(h^{(1)}\), then into \(h^{(2)}\), and so on until the output score \(s_\theta(x)\) is produced. There are no feedback loops in this description: later layers do not feed their outputs back into earlier layers. Each layer receives input from the previous layer and passes its output forward.



35.0.8 Question 7
For a classification network with a single hidden width \(H=8\) and \(K=3\) classes, the final affine layer has \[
s_\theta(x)=Vh+c.
\] State the dimensions of \(V\), \(c\), and \(s_\theta(x)\).


Answer

The hidden representation satisfies \[
h\in\mathbb R^8.
\] To produce \(K=3\) logits, \[
V\in\mathbb R^{3\times8},
\qquad
c\in\mathbb R^3.
\] Then \[
Vh+c\in\mathbb R^3.
\] Thus \[
s_\theta(x)\in\mathbb R^3.
\]



35.0.9 Question 8
The lecture says classification network outputs are often treated as logits. What is a logit in this context, and why are logits not probabilities?


Answer

A logit is a raw class score produced by the final affine layer of the network. For \(K\) classes, the logit vector is \[
s_\theta(x)\in\mathbb R^K.
\] Logits are not probabilities because their entries can be negative, positive, or zero, and they do not have to sum to one. To obtain probabilities, one applies the softmax function: \[
p_\theta(x)=\operatorname{softmax}(s_\theta(x)).
\]



35.0.10 Question 9
A classifier has logits \[
s=(0,\log 2,\log 3).
\] Compute the softmax probability vector.


Answer

Softmax probabilities are \[
p_k=\frac{e^{s_k}}{\sum_j e^{s_j}}.
\] Here \[
e^0=1,
\qquad
e^{\log2}=2,
\qquad
e^{\log3}=3.
\] The denominator is \(1+2+3=6\). Therefore \[
p=\left(\frac16,\frac26,\frac36\right)=\left(\frac16,\frac13,\frac12\right).
\]



35.0.11 Question 10
A network architecture has \(D=20\) inputs, hidden widths \[
\quad d_1=10,
\quad d_2=5,
\] and outputs \(K=4\) logits. Compute the total number of parameters.


Answer

The \(20\to10\) layer has \[
10\cdot20+10=210
\] parameters.
The \(10\to5\) layer has \[
5\cdot10+5=55
\] parameters.
The \(5\to4\) layer has \[
4\cdot5+4=24
\] parameters.
The total is \[
210+55+24=289.
\]



35.0.12 Question 11
For one-hidden-layer classification, \[
h=\phi(Wx+b),\qquad s_\theta(x)=Vh+c,
\] with \(K\) classes and \(H\) hidden units. Derive the shapes of \(W\), \(b\), \(V\), and \(c\) when \(x\in\mathbb R^D\).


Answer

The hidden layer maps \(\mathbb R^D\) to \(\mathbb R^H\), so \[
W\in\mathbb R^{H\times D},
\qquad
b\in\mathbb R^H.
\] Then \[
h=\phi(Wx+b)\in\mathbb R^H.
\] The output layer maps \(\mathbb R^H\) to \(\mathbb R^K\), so \[
V\in\mathbb R^{K\times H},
\qquad
c\in\mathbb R^K.
\] Thus \[
s_\theta(x)=Vh+c\in\mathbb R^K.
\]



35.0.13 Question 12
For predicted class probabilities \[
p=(0.1,0.7,0.2)
\] and true class \(y=2\), compute the categorical cross-entropy loss. Use natural logarithms.


Answer

The correct-class probability is \[
p_y=p_2=0.7.
\] The loss is \[
-\log(p_y)=-\log(0.7)\approx 0.357.
\]



35.0.14 Question 13
Suppose a hidden layer uses ReLU activation, \(\phi(t)=\max\{0,t\}\) componentwise. For pre-activation vector \[
z=(-2,0,3),
\] compute the hidden representation \(h=\phi(z)\).


Answer

Apply ReLU to each coordinate: \[
\phi(-2)=0,
\qquad
\phi(0)=0,
\qquad
\phi(3)=3.
\] Thus \[
h=(0,0,3).
\]



35.0.15 Question 14
A hidden layer maps \(\mathbb R^4\) to \(\mathbb R^3\) using an affine map and an activation. How many weights and biases does this layer have?


Answer

Here \(d_{i-1}=4\) and \(d_i=3\). The weight matrix has \[
3\cdot4=12
\] entries. The bias vector has \[
3
\] entries. The layer has \[
12+3=15
\] parameters.



35.0.16 Question 15
For a classification network with logits \[
s=(2,1,0),
\] Which class is predicted? Does applying softmax change the predicted class?


Answer

The largest logit is the first entry, \(2\), so the predicted class is class \(1\) if classes are indexed as \(1,2,3\). Applying softmax does not change the predicted class because softmax is monotone in each logit relative to the others: the largest logit gets the largest softmax probability.



35.0.17 Question 16
Why does the lecture describe neural networks as learning intermediate representations?


Answer

Each hidden layer produces a new representation of the input, such as \[
h^{(1)}=s_1(x),
\qquad
h^{(2)}=s_2(h^{(1)}).
\] These representations are not fixed before training; they depend on learned weights and biases. The final layer then makes predictions from the last learned representation.
Thus the network learns both the features and the final prediction rule, rather than fitting a linear model to a fixed feature representation supplied in advance.

title: 36  Training Neural Networks with Backpropagation - Review Questions
text:
Warning: AI-assisted materials These materials were developed with assistance from AI tools. Students should treat these materials as instructor-reviewed course content while applying the same critical judgment they would use with any technical material. Please report any suspected errors or unclear explanations to ghunt@wm.edu.


36.0.1 Question 1
State what remains the same and what changes when the lecture moves from linear/logistic regression to neural-network training. Your answer should mention the empirical risk, the score function, and the optimization problem.


Answer

The ERM structure is unchanged: choose a score function, choose a loss, and minimize
\[
\hat R(\theta)=\frac1N\sum_{n=1}^N \ell(y_n,s_\theta(x_n)).
\]
What changes is the score class. Instead of a linear score, the model uses a layered composition
\[
s_\theta(x)=s_L(s_{L-1}(\cdots s_1(x)\cdots)),
\]
with many parameters across layers. The resulting optimization problem is usually nonconvex and generally has no closed-form solution, so gradient-based iterative methods are used.



36.0.2 Question 2
For the one-hidden-unit model
\[
a_n=wx_n+b,\qquad h_n=\sigma(a_n),\qquad s_n=vh_n+c,
\]
with empirical risk
\[
\hat{R}(\theta)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^N \frac{1}{2}(y_n-s_n)^2
\]
derive the gradients
\[
\frac{\partial \hat{R}}{\partial v},\qquad
\frac{\partial \hat{R}}{\partial c},\qquad
\frac{\partial \hat{R}}{\partial w},\qquad
\frac{\partial \hat{R}}{\partial b}
\]
using the chain rule.
Hint: Work first with one observation,
\[
\ell_n=\frac{1}{2}(y_n-s_n)^2.
\]
Use the paths
\[
\ell_n \to s_n \to v,\qquad
\ell_n \to s_n \to c,\qquad
\ell_n \to s_n \to h_n \to a_n \to w,\qquad
\ell_n \to s_n \to h_n \to a_n \to b.
\]
Compute the intermediate derivatives
\[
\frac{\partial \ell_n}{\partial s_n},\quad
\frac{\partial s_n}{\partial v},\quad
\frac{\partial s_n}{\partial c},\quad
\frac{\partial s_n}{\partial h_n},\quad
\frac{\partial h_n}{\partial a_n},\quad
\frac{\partial a_n}{\partial w},\quad
\frac{\partial a_n}{\partial b},
\]
then average over \(n=1,...,N\).


Answer

Let
\[
e_n=s_n-y_n.
\]
Since
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial s_n}\left(\frac{1}{2}(y_n-s_n)^2\right)
=s_n-y_n=e_n,
\]
we have
\[
\frac{\partial \hat{R}}{\partial v}
=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^N e_n h_n,
\qquad
\frac{\partial \hat{R}}{\partial c}
=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^N e_n.
\]
Also,
\[
\frac{\partial s_n}{\partial h_n}=v,
\qquad
\frac{\partial h_n}{\partial a_n}=h_n(1-h_n),
\qquad
\frac{\partial a_n}{\partial w}=x_n,
\qquad
\frac{\partial a_n}{\partial b}=1.
\]
Therefore
\[
\frac{\partial \hat{R}}{\partial w}
=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^N e_n v h_n(1-h_n)x_n,
\qquad
\frac{\partial \hat{R}}{\partial b}
=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^N e_n v h_n(1-h_n).
\]



36.0.3 Question 3
Recompute the forward pass for
\[
x=2,\quad y=1,\quad w=0.5,\quad b=0.1,\quad v=1.5,\quad c=-0.2,
\]
using \(a=wx+b\), \(h=\sigma(a)\), \(s=vh+c\), and \(L=\frac12(y-s)^2\).


Answer

The pre-activation is
\[
a=(0.5)(2)+0.1=1.1.
\]
Thus
\[
h=\sigma(1.1)=\frac1{1+e^{-1.1}}\approx 0.7503.
\]
The score is
\[
s=(1.5)(0.7503)-0.2\approx 0.9254.
\]
Finally,
\[
L=\frac12(1-0.9254)^2\approx 0.0028.
\]



36.0.4 Question 4
Carry the backward pass through the same scalar example from Question 4. Compute
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial s},\quad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial v},\quad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial c},\quad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial h},\quad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial a},\quad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial w},\quad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial b}.
\]


Answer

From the forward pass, \(h\approx0.7503\) and \(s\approx0.9254\). The loss derivative is
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial s}=s-y\approx -0.0746.
\]
For \(s=vh+c\),
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial v}=(-0.0746)(0.7503)\approx -0.0560,
\qquad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial c}= -0.0746,
\]
and
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial h}=(-0.0746)(1.5)\approx -0.1119.
\]
For \(h=\sigma(a)\),
\[
\frac{\partial h}{\partial a}=h(1-h)\approx(0.7503)(0.2497)\approx0.1874,
\]
so
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial a}\approx(-0.1119)(0.1874)\approx -0.0210.
\]
For \(a=wx+b\) with \(x=2\),
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial w}\approx(-0.0210)(2)=-0.0419,
\qquad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial b}\approx -0.0210.
\]



36.0.5 Question 5
After the backward pass in Question 5, gradient descent with learning rate \(\eta>0\) updates \(w\) by
\[
w^{(t+1)}=w^{(t)}-\eta \frac{\partial L}{\partial w}.
\]
Does this step increase or decrease \(w\) in the numerical example?


Answer

Here
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial w}\approx -0.0419<0.
\]
Therefore
\[
w^{(t+1)}=w^{(t)}-\eta(-0.0419)=w^{(t)}+0.0419\eta.
\]
For any \(\eta>0\), the update increases \(w\). This is consistent with moving opposite the gradient: a negative derivative means increasing \(w\) locally reduces the loss.



36.0.6 Question 6
Classify the update rule by its batch size. For a dataset of size \(N\), identify which case is full-batch gradient descent, which is strict stochastic gradient descent, and which is mini-batch gradient descent:
\[
|B_t|=N,\qquad |B_t|=1,\qquad 1<|B_t|<N.
\]


Answer

If \(|B_t|=N\), the update uses every training observation, so it is full-batch gradient descent.
If \(|B_t|=1\), the update uses one randomly selected observation, so it is stochastic gradient descent in the strict sense.
If \(1<|B_t|<N\), the update uses a subset larger than one but smaller than the whole dataset, so it is mini-batch gradient descent. As the lecture notes, neural-network practice often uses “SGD” broadly to include this mini-batch case.



36.0.7 Question 7
Assume a mini-batch of size \(B\) is sampled uniformly with replacement from the training indices \({1,\dots,N}\). Let \(k_1,\dots,k_B\) denote the sampled indices, and define the mini-batch gradient as
\[
\hat g_B=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{j=1}^B \nabla_\theta \ell(y_{k_j},s_\theta(x_{k_j})).
\]
Show that the expected value of this mini-batch gradient equals the full empirical-risk gradient:
\[
\mathbb E[\hat g_B]=\nabla_\theta \hat R(\theta).
\]


Answer

For each training observation, define its individual gradient contribution as
\[
g_i=\nabla_\theta \ell(y_i,s_\theta(x_i)).
\]
Since \(k_1,\dots,k_B\) are sampled uniformly with replacement from \({1,\dots,N}\), each sampled index \(k_j\) has the same distribution. Therefore, for each draw,
\[
\mathbb E[g_{k_j}]=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N g_i.
\]
The mini-batch gradient can be written as
\[
\hat g_B=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{j=1}^B g_{k_j}.
\]
By linearity of expectation,
\[
\mathbb E[\hat g_B]=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{j=1}^B \mathbb E[g_{k_j}].
\]
Substituting the expression for each \(\mathbb E[g_{k_j}]\) gives
\[
\mathbb E[\hat g_B]=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{j=1}^B \left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N g_i\right).
\]
Since the same quantity is added \(B\) times,
\[
\mathbb E[\hat g_B]=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N g_i.
\]
Now,
\[
\hat R(\theta)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \ell(y_i,s_\theta(x_i)).
\]
Taking the gradient gives
\[
\nabla_\theta \hat R(\theta)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \nabla_\theta \ell(y_i,s_\theta(x_i)).
\]
Using the definition of \(g_i\), this becomes
\[
\nabla_\theta \hat R(\theta)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N g_i.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\mathbb E[\hat g_B]=\nabla_\theta \hat R(\theta).
\]



36.0.8 Question 8
Suppose there are \(N=1250\) training observations and the mini-batch size is \(64\). How many updates are in one epoch if the algorithm uses every observation once and includes a final smaller mini-batch?


Answer

The exact number of updates is
\[
\left\lceil \frac{1250}{64}\right\rceil=20.
\]
There are \(19\) full mini-batches of size \(64\), which use \(19\cdot64=1216\) observations. This leaves \(1250-1216=34\) observations for one final smaller mini-batch.
So one epoch has \(20\) updates. The rough calculation \(1250/64\approx19.5\) suggests about \(20\) updates, and the exact count is \(20\) when the final partial mini-batch is included.



36.0.9 Question 9
In the chain
\[
x\to q\to r\to t\to u\to L,
\]
show explicitly how reusing \(\partial L/\partial r\) avoids recomputing the full chain-rule expression for \(\partial L/\partial q\).


Answer

The full chain-rule expression is
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial q}=
\frac{\partial L}{\partial u}
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}
\frac{\partial t}{\partial r}
\frac{\partial r}{\partial q}.
\]
But the first three factors are exactly
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial r}=
\frac{\partial L}{\partial u}
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}
\frac{\partial t}{\partial r}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial q}=
\frac{\partial L}{\partial r}\frac{\partial r}{\partial q}.
\]
Backpropagation stores or passes the already-computed derivative \(\partial L/\partial r\) and multiplies by only the next local derivative.



36.0.10 Question 10
At a single node \(r=f(q)\), suppose the upstream gradient is
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial r}=5,
\]
and \(f(q)=q^3\) at \(q=2\). Compute the downstream gradient \(\partial L/\partial q\).


Answer

The local derivative is
\[
\frac{\partial r}{\partial q}=f'(q)=3q^2.
\]
At \(q=2\),
\[
\frac{\partial r}{\partial q}=3(2)^2=12.
\]
The downstream gradient is upstream times local derivative:
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial q}=
\frac{\partial L}{\partial r}\frac{\partial r}{\partial q}
=5\cdot12=60.
\]



36.0.11 Question 11
Combine the local derivatives in the scalar graph to obtain a single formula for \(\partial J/\partial \alpha\) for one observation. Use
\[
J=\frac{1}{4}(u-t)^4,\qquad u=\gamma r+\delta,\qquad r=\tanh(q),\qquad q=\alpha z+\beta.
\]
Note: \(\tanh'(q)=1-\tanh^2(q).\)


Answer

The path from \(\alpha\) to \(J\) is
\[
\alpha \to q \to r \to u \to J.
\]
The chain rule gives
\[
\frac{\partial J}{\partial \alpha}=\frac{\partial J}{\partial u}\frac{\partial u}{\partial r}\frac{\partial r}{\partial q}\frac{\partial q}{\partial \alpha}.
\]
The local derivatives are
\[
\frac{\partial J}{\partial u}=(u-t)^3,\qquad \frac{\partial u}{\partial r}=\gamma,\qquad \frac{\partial r}{\partial q}=\tanh'(q),\qquad \frac{\partial q}{\partial \alpha}=z.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\frac{\partial J}{\partial \alpha}=(u-t)^3\gamma\tanh'(q)z.
\]
Since \(\tanh'(q)=1-\tanh^2(q)\) and \(r=\tanh(q)\), this can also be written as
\[
\frac{\partial J}{\partial \alpha}=(u-t)^3\gamma(1-r^2)z.
\]



36.0.12 Question 12
For a mini-batch \(B\) of scalar observations, let \(M=|B|\) and define
\[
J_B=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{n\in B} L_n,
\]
where
\[
L_n=\frac{1}{4}(u_n-t_n)^4,\qquad u_n=\gamma r_n+\delta,\qquad r_n=\tanh(q_n),\qquad q_n=\alpha z_n+\beta.
\]
Write the gradients of \(J_B\) with respect to \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta\).


Answer

Since
\[
J_B=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{n\in B} L_n,
\]
each parameter gradient is the average of the corresponding single-observation gradients. First compute
\[
\frac{\partial L_n}{\partial u_n}=(u_n-t_n)^3.
\]
For compactness, define
\[
d_n=(u_n-t_n)^3.
\]
For \(\gamma\), the chain rule gives
\[
\frac{\partial L_n}{\partial \gamma}=\frac{\partial L_n}{\partial u_n}\frac{\partial u_n}{\partial \gamma}=d_n r_n.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\frac{\partial J_B}{\partial \gamma}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{n\in B} d_n r_n.
\]
For \(\delta\), the chain rule gives
\[
\frac{\partial L_n}{\partial \delta}=\frac{\partial L_n}{\partial u_n}\frac{\partial u_n}{\partial \delta}=d_n.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\frac{\partial J_B}{\partial \delta}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{n\in B} d_n.
\]
For \(\alpha\), the path is \(\alpha\to q_n\to r_n\to u_n\to L_n\). The chain rule gives
\[
\frac{\partial L_n}{\partial \alpha}=\frac{\partial L_n}{\partial u_n}\frac{\partial u_n}{\partial r_n}\frac{\partial r_n}{\partial q_n}\frac{\partial q_n}{\partial \alpha}=d_n\gamma\tanh'(q_n)z_n.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\frac{\partial J_B}{\partial \alpha}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{n\in B} d_n\gamma\tanh'(q_n)z_n.
\]
For \(\beta\), the path is \(\beta\to q_n\to r_n\to u_n\to L_n\). The chain rule gives
\[
\frac{\partial L_n}{\partial \beta}=\frac{\partial L_n}{\partial u_n}\frac{\partial u_n}{\partial r_n}\frac{\partial r_n}{\partial q_n}\frac{\partial q_n}{\partial \beta}=d_n\gamma\tanh'(q_n).
\]
Therefore,
\[
\frac{\partial J_B}{\partial \beta}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{n\in B} d_n\gamma\tanh'(q_n).
\]
Since \(\tanh'(q_n)=1-\tanh^2(q_n)\) and \(r_n=\tanh(q_n)\), the last two gradients can also be written as
\[
\frac{\partial J_B}{\partial \alpha}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{n\in B} d_n\gamma(1-r_n^2)z_n,
\]
and
\[
\frac{\partial J_B}{\partial \beta}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{n\in B} d_n\gamma(1-r_n^2).
\]



36.0.13 Question 13
For the mini-batch objective
\[
J_B=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{n\in B}L_n,\qquad L_n=\frac{1}{4}(u_n-t_n)^4,
\]
with
\[
u_n=\gamma r_n+\delta,\qquad r_n=\tanh(q_n),\qquad q_n=\alpha z_n+\beta,
\]
why do the gradients for the shared parameters \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta\) sum contributions over the mini-batch, while quantities such as \(\partial J_B/\partial r_n\) and \(\partial J_B/\partial q_n\) are kept separately for each observation before continuing backward?


Answer

The parameters \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta\) are shared across all observations in the mini-batch. The same value of \(\gamma\), for example, appears in every expression
\[
u_n=\gamma r_n+\delta.
\]
Therefore, the total derivative of \(J_B\) with respect to \(\gamma\) must add the contributions from every observation:
\[
\frac{\partial J_B}{\partial \gamma}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{n\in B}\frac{\partial L_n}{\partial u_n}\frac{\partial u_n}{\partial \gamma}.
\]
Using \(d_n=(u_n-t_n)^3\) and \(\partial u_n/\partial \gamma=r_n\), this becomes
\[
\frac{\partial J_B}{\partial \gamma}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{n\in B}d_n r_n.
\]
The same idea applies to the other shared parameters. For example,
\[
\frac{\partial J_B}{\partial \delta}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{n\in B}d_n,
\]
and
\[
\frac{\partial J_B}{\partial \alpha}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{n\in B}d_n\gamma\tanh'(q_n)z_n,\qquad
\frac{\partial J_B}{\partial \beta}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{n\in B}d_n\gamma\tanh'(q_n).
\]
By contrast, \(r_n\) and \(q_n\) are not shared parameters. They are intermediate values for a specific observation \(n\). Before the backward pass can continue from \(r_n\) to \(q_n\), it needs one derivative for each observation:
\[
\frac{\partial J_B}{\partial r_n}=\frac{1}{M}d_n\gamma.
\]
Then, for each observation separately,
\[
\frac{\partial J_B}{\partial q_n}=\frac{\partial J_B}{\partial r_n}\frac{\partial r_n}{\partial q_n}=\frac{1}{M}d_n\gamma\tanh'(q_n).
\]
So the rule is: gradients for shared parameters are summed over the mini-batch, while gradients for per-observation intermediate quantities remain indexed by \(n\) until they are used by the next local backward rule.



36.0.14 Question 14
When a graph branches, gradient contributions add. Verify this in the concrete graph
\[
r=z^2,\qquad t=z^3,\qquad L=r+t.
\]
Compute \(\partial L/\partial z\) by adding path contributions, and compare with direct differentiation.


Answer

There are two downstream paths from \(z\) to \(L\). The contribution through \(r\) is
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial r}\frac{\partial r}{\partial z}=1\cdot 2z=2z.
\]
The contribution through \(t\) is
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial t}\frac{\partial t}{\partial z}=1\cdot 3z^2=3z^2.
\]
Adding gives
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial z}=2z+3z^2.
\]
Directly, \(L=z^2+z^3\), so
\[
\frac{dL}{dz}=2z+3z^2.
\]
The two calculations agree.



36.0.15 Question 15
A dense layer has
\[
Z=XW+b,
\]
where \(X\in\mathbb R^{B\times d}\), \(W\in\mathbb R^{d\times m}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and the upstream gradient is
\[
G=\frac{\partial L}{\partial Z}\in\mathbb R^{B\times m}.
\]
State the shapes of
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial X},\qquad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial W},\qquad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial b},
\]
look the dense-layer backward formulas from the lecture, and check that the right-hand side of each formula has the correct shape.


Answer

Each gradient has the same shape as the quantity it differentiates:
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial X}\in\mathbb R^{B\times d},\qquad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial W}\in\mathbb R^{d\times m},\qquad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial b}\in\mathbb R^m.
\]
The dense-layer backward formulas are
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial X}=GW^T,\qquad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial W}=X^TG,\qquad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial b}=\sum_{i=1}^B G_i,
\]
where \(G_i\) is row \(i\) of \(G\).
Now check the shapes. Since \(G\in\mathbb R^{B\times m}\) and \(W^T\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}\),
\[
GW^T\in\mathbb R^{B\times d},
\]
which matches the shape of \(X\).
Since \(X^T\in\mathbb R^{d\times B}\) and \(G\in\mathbb R^{B\times m}\),
\[
X^TG\in\mathbb R^{d\times m},
\]
which matches the shape of \(W\).
Finally, summing \(G\in\mathbb R^{B\times m}\) over the \(B\) batch rows gives a vector in \(\mathbb R^m\):
\[
\sum_{i=1}^B G_i\in\mathbb R^m,
\]
which matches the shape of \(b\).



36.0.16 Question 16
Suppose flattening tensors gives \(X\) with shape \(20\times120\) and \(Y\) with shape \(20\times60\). What is the shape of the Jacobian
\[
J=\frac{\partial \operatorname{vec}(Y)}{\partial \operatorname{vec}(X)},
\]
and how many entries does it contain?


Answer

The flattened input has
\[
n=20\cdot120=2400
\]
entries, and the flattened output has
\[
m=20\cdot60=1200
\]
entries. Therefore,
\[
J\in\mathbb R^{1200\times2400}.
\]
The number of entries is
\[
1200\cdot2400=2{,}880{,}000.
\]
This is why the lecture emphasizes computing VJPs directly rather than explicitly forming \(J\).



36.0.17 Question 17
Consider the quadratic objective
\[
R(\theta)=\frac{1}{2}\theta^2.
\]
For this objective, the gradient is
\[
R'(\theta)=\theta.
\]
Gradient descent with learning rate \(\eta\) therefore gives the update
\[
\theta^{(t+1)}=\theta^{(t)}-\eta \theta^{(t)}.
\]

What is the formula for \(\theta^{(t)}\) in terms of \(\theta^{(0)}\)?
For which values of \(\eta\) does \(\theta^{(t)}\) converge to \(0\)?



Answer

Starting from
\[
\theta^{(t+1)}=\theta^{(t)}-\eta\theta^{(t)},
\]
factor out \(\theta^{(t)}\):
\[
\theta^{(t+1)}=(1-\eta)\theta^{(t)}.
\]
So in the form \(\theta^{(t+1)}=a\theta^{(t)}\), we have
\[
a=1-\eta.
\]
Applying the update repeatedly gives
\[
\theta^{(t)}=(1-\eta)^t\theta^{(0)}.
\]
This converges to \(0\) exactly when the multiplier \(1-\eta\) has absolute value less than \(1\):
\[
|1-\eta|<1.
\]
Solving this inequality gives
\[
-1<1-\eta<1.
\]
Subtracting \(1\) from all three parts gives
\[
-2<-\eta<0.
\]
Multiplying by \(-1\) reverses the inequalities:
\[
0<\eta<2.
\]
Therefore, gradient descent converges to \(0\) for learning rates satisfying
\[
0<\eta<2.
\]
If \(\eta>2\), then \(|1-\eta|>1\), so the iterates grow in magnitude. This is the precise sense in which a learning rate that is too large can make gradient descent unstable.



36.0.18 Question 18
Changing the mini-batch objective from an average
\[
\frac1{|B_t|}\sum_{n\in B_t}\ell_n(\theta)
\]
to a sum
\[
\sum_{n\in B_t}\ell_n(\theta)
\]
would change the gradient used in the update. What exactly changes, and why does the averaging convention make learning-rate comparisons across batch sizes cleaner?


Answer

The gradient of the sum is \(|B_t|\) times the gradient of the average:
\[
\nabla_\theta\sum_{n\in B_t}\ell_n(\theta)
=|B_t|\nabla_\theta\left(\frac1{|B_t|}\sum_{n\in B_t}\ell_n(\theta)\right).
\]
With the same learning rate, using the summed loss would therefore make the step size scale linearly with the batch size. Averaging keeps the gradient on roughly the same scale when \(|B_t|\) changes, so the learning rate has a more comparable meaning across different mini-batch sizes.

37.0.1 Question 1
Give one precise way in which each of the following can increase model flexibility: depth, width, and amount of training.


Answer

Increasing depth adds more composed transformations, so the network can build more complex hierarchical representations. Increasing width adds more units in a layer, so the layer can represent more features or directions at once. Increasing the amount of training can let the optimizer fit the empirical risk more closely.
Greater flexibility can increase the opportunity to overfit, but test performance also depends on the data, architecture, regularization, optimization bias, and validation-based model selection. Over-parameterized models may still generalize well, so flexibility alone does not determine test error.



37.0.2 Question 2
A dense layer maps \(s_i:\mathbb R^{d_{i-1}}\to\mathbb R^{d_i}\) using
\[
h^{(i)}=\phi_i(W^{(i)}h^{(i-1)}+b^{(i)}).
\]
How many trainable parameters does this layer have including the weights \(W^{(i)}\) and bias term \(b^{(i)}\).


Answer

The weight matrix has shape
\[
W^{(i)}\in\mathbb R^{d_i\times d_{i-1}},
\]
so it contains \(d_i d_{i-1}\) scalar weights. The bias vector has shape
\[
b^{(i)}\in\mathbb R^{d_i},
\]
so it contains \(d_i\) scalar biases. Therefore the dense layer has
\[
d_i d_{i-1}+d_i
\]
trainable parameters.



37.0.3 Question 3
For the lecture’s parameter-count example with \(D=20\) input features, one hidden layer of width \(H=50\), and one scalar output, compute the number of parameters in the hidden layer, the output layer, and the full network. Compare this with a linear regression model with 20 predictors and an intercept.


Answer

The hidden layer has
\[
50\cdot20+50=1050
\]
parameters. The scalar output layer has
\[
1\cdot50+1=51
\]
parameters. The full network therefore has
\[
1050+51=1101
\]
parameters.
A linear regression model with 20 predictors and an intercept has \(20+1=21\) parameters. The neural network has many more parameters because it learns hidden features before the final scalar output.



37.0.4 Question 4
A weight-decay-style update in the lecture is
\[
\theta^{(t+1)}=(1-\eta\lambda)\theta^{(t)}-\eta\nabla_\theta\hat R(\theta^{(t)}).
\]
Which penalized objective gives exactly this update under ordinary gradient descent: \(\hat R(\theta)+\lambda\|\theta\|_2^2\) or \(\hat R(\theta)+\frac{\lambda}{2}\|\theta\|_2^2\)? Justify your answer.


Answer

The objective
\[
\hat R(\theta)+\frac{\lambda}{2}\|\theta\|_2^2
\]
has gradient
\[
\nabla_\theta\hat R(\theta)+\lambda\theta.
\]
Gradient descent gives
\[
\theta^{(t+1)}=\theta^{(t)}-
\eta\{\nabla_\theta\hat R(\theta^{(t)})+\lambda\theta^{(t)}\}
=(1-\eta\lambda)\theta^{(t)}-
\eta\nabla_\theta\hat R(\theta^{(t)}).
\]
If the objective were \(\hat R(\theta)+\lambda\|\theta\|_2^2\), the penalty gradient would be \(2\lambda\theta\), giving a factor \(1-2\eta\lambda\) instead.



37.0.5 Question 5
For inverted dropout, the lecture defines
\[
m_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1-p),\qquad
\tilde h_i=\frac{m_i h_i}{1-p}.
\]
Verify that \(\mathbb E[\tilde h_i]=h_i\).


Answer

Since \(m_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1-p)\),
\[
\mathbb E[m_i]=1-p.
\]
Treating \(h_i\) as fixed during the dropout draw,
\[
\mathbb E[\tilde h_i]
=\mathbb E\left[\frac{m_i h_i}{1-p}\right]
=\frac{h_i}{1-p}\mathbb E[m_i]
=\frac{h_i}{1-p}(1-p)
=h_i.
\]
Thus inverted dropout preserves the activation’s expected scale during training.



37.0.6 Question 6
Take \(h_i=3\) and dropout probability \(p=0.25\). Under inverted dropout, what values can \(\tilde h_i\) take, and with what probabilities? Compute its mean and variance.


Answer

The unit is dropped with probability \(p=0.25\), so \(\tilde h_i=0\) with probability \(0.25\). It is kept with probability \(1-p=0.75\), and then
\[
\tilde h_i=\frac{3}{0.75}=4.
\]
The mean is
\[
0(0.25)+4(0.75)=3.
\]
The variance can be computed directly:
\[
0.25(0-3)^2+0.75(4-3)^2
=0.25\cdot9+0.75\cdot1=3.
\]



37.0.7 Question 7
Classify each training pattern as more suggestive of underfitting, overfitting, or reasonable fit. Use the lecture’s emphasis on training and validation performance.

Training loss high, validation loss high.
Training loss low, validation loss much higher and worsening.
Training loss low, validation loss low and stable.



Answer


High training and validation loss suggests underfitting: the model is not fitting even the training data well.
Low training loss but much higher and worsening validation loss suggests overfitting: continued training is fitting training-set idiosyncrasies rather than improving generalization.
Low training loss and low stable validation loss suggests a reasonable fit, at least relative to the available validation data.

The diagnosis is based on the gap and trend between training and validation performance, not training performance alone.



37.0.8 Question 8
In early stopping, why should the validation set be used to decide when to stop, while the test set should be reserved until after model selection is complete?


Answer

The validation set is part of the model-selection procedure: it helps choose when to stop training and, more generally, tune hyperparameters. If the test set were used for that choice, then information from the test set would influence the fitted model or training procedure.
The test set is meant to estimate performance on new data after all model-selection decisions are finished. Keeping it separate gives a less biased final estimate of generalization performance.



37.0.9 Question 9
Suppose each feature \(x_j\) is standardized using a mean \(\bar x_j\) and standard deviation \(s_j\):
\[
x_j\mapsto \frac{x_j-\bar x_j}{s_j}.
\]
A student computes \(\bar x_j\) and \(s_j\) using the full dataset before splitting the data into training, validation, and test sets.
Explain why this is a form of data leakage. Then state the correct procedure for computing and applying \(\bar x_j\) and \(s_j\).


Answer

This is data leakage because the preprocessing step uses information from observations that are supposed to be held out for validation or testing. Even though the labels are not used, the feature distributions from the validation and test sets influence the values of \(\bar x_j\) and \(s_j\). Those values are then used to transform the training data before the model is fit.
The correct procedure is:

Split the data into training, validation, and test sets.
Compute \(\bar x_j\) and \(s_j\) using only the training set.
Treat those values as fixed preprocessing parameters.
Apply the same transformation to the training, validation, and test observations:

\[
x_j\mapsto \frac{x_j-\bar x_j}{s_j}.
\]
The validation and test sets should be transformed using the training-set mean and standard deviation, not their own means and standard deviations.



37.0.10 Question 10
In SGD with momentum, suppose
\[
v_t=\rho v_{t-1}+g_t,
\qquad v_0=0,
\]
and \(g_t=g\) is the same vector for every step. Derive \(v_t\) in closed form.


Answer

Expanding the recursion gives
\[
v_1=g,
\]
\[
v_2=\rho g+g=(1+\rho)g,
\]
and in general
\[
v_t=(1+\rho+\rho^2+\cdots+\rho^{t-1})g.
\]
For \(\rho\ne1\),
\[
v_t=\frac{1-\rho^t}{1-\rho}g.
\]
If \(0\le \rho<1\), then \(v_t\to g/(1-\rho)\) as \(t\to\infty\).



37.0.11 Question 11
Compute one RMSProp update in one dimension. Let \(\theta^{(t)}=2\), \(g_t=4\), \(s_{t-1}=9\), \(\rho=0.9\), \(\eta=0.01\), and ignore \(\epsilon\) for simplicity.


Answer

First compute the squared-gradient average:
\[
s_t=0.9(9)+0.1(4^2)=8.1+1.6=9.7.
\]
Then
\[
\sqrt{s_t}=\sqrt{9.7}\approx3.114.
\]
The update is
\[
\theta^{(t+1)}=2-0.01\frac{4}{3.114}
\approx2-0.01285=1.98715.
\]



37.0.12 Question 12
Using the lecture’s simplified Adam update, take \(m_{t-1}=0\), \(s_{t-1}=0\), \(g_t=2\), \(\beta_1=0.9\), \(\beta_2=0.99\), \(\eta=0.001\), and ignore \(\epsilon\). Compute the updated used in the Adam update to the parameters.


Answer

The first moment is
\[
m_t=0.9(0)+(1-0.9)(2)=0.2.
\]
The squared-gradient average is
\[
s_t=0.99(0)+(1-0.99)(2^2)=0.04.
\]
Thus
\[
\sqrt{s_t}=0.2.
\]
The update size is (ignoring \(\epsilon\))
\[
\eta\frac{m_t}{\sqrt{s_t}}
=0.001\frac{0.2}{0.2}=0.001.
\]



37.0.13 Question 13
For the MNIST Keras model in the lecture, compute the trainable parameter count by layer:

Flattened input length \(784\) to dense layer of width \(128\).
Dense layer of width \(128\) to dense layer of width \(64\).
Dense layer of width \(64\) to softmax output layer of width \(10\).

Verify the total \(109{,}386\).


Answer

The first dense layer has
\[
784\cdot128+128=100352+128=100480
\]
parameters. The second dense layer has
\[
128\cdot64+64=8192+64=8256
\]
parameters. The output layer has
\[
64\cdot10+10=640+10=650
\]
parameters. Dropout and flattening have no trainable parameters. The total is
\[
100480+8256+650=109386.
\]



37.0.14 Question 14
Give a precise distinction between an over-parameterized model and an overfit model.


Answer

A model is over-parameterized when it has many parameters, possibly enough to fit the training data extremely well. This is a statement about model size and capacity relative to the data.
A model is overfit when it generalizes poorly: it performs much better on training data than on new data. This is a statement about the gap between training performance and out-of-sample performance.



37.0.15 Question 15
Name three reasons why an over-parameterized neural network can still generalize well.


Answer

First, architecture imposes structure: the model is not an arbitrary function.
Second, explicit regularization can help: the example uses dropout and an \(L_2\) kernel regularizer on a dense layer.
Third, optimization can have implicit regularizing effects: gradient-based methods such as Adam do not choose an arbitrary parameter setting but follow a particular training trajectory determined by initialization, mini-batches, gradients, and update rules.



37.0.16 Question 16
A student summarizes double descent as: “Once a model is past the interpolation threshold, making it larger always improves test error.” Explain why this is not what the lecture claims.


Answer

The lecture says that in some modern machine-learning settings, test error may decrease again after the interpolation threshold. It explicitly does not claim that larger models are always better.
Double descent is a possible pattern, not a universal monotonic guarantee. Test error still depends on the data-generating process, architecture, optimization, regularization, noise, and the way model complexity is measured. The safer conclusion is that parameter count alone is not enough to determine whether a model will overfit.

title: 38  Principal Component Analysis (PCA) - Review Questions
text:

38.0.1 Question 1
List the dimensions of the four objects \(W\), \(P_W\), \(Z=XW\), and \(XP_W\) when \(X\in\mathbb R^{N\times D}\) and \(W\in\mathbb R^{D\times q}\) has full column rank. State which of \(Z\) and \(XP_W\) is written in principal-component coordinates and which is written in the original variable coordinates.


Answer

The matrix \(W\) has shape \(D\times q\) and its columns form a basis for the chosen \(q\)-dimensional subspace. The projection matrix
\[
P_W=W(W^TW)^{-1}W^T
\]
has shape \(D\times D\) and projects row vectors in \(\mathbb R^D\) onto \(\operatorname{Col}(W)\).
The score matrix
\[
Z=XW
\]
has shape \(N\times q\) and gives the data in the new \(q\)-dimensional coordinates. The projected data
\[
XP_W
\]
has shape \(N\times D\) and gives the projected observations written back in the original \(D\) coordinates.



38.0.2 Question 2
Verify the lecture’s orthonormal-basis shortcut. If the columns of \(W\in\mathbb R^{D\times q}\) are orthonormal, compute \(W^TW\) and prove that \(P_W=WW^T\) is both symmetric \(P_W^T = P_W\) and idempotent \(P_W^2 = P_W\).


Answer

Orthonormal columns mean \(w_i^T w_j=0\) for \(i\ne j\) and \(w_i^T w_i=1\), so
\[
W^TW=I_q.
\]
Therefore
\[
P_W=W(W^TW)^{-1}W^T=W I_q W^T=WW^T.
\]
It is symmetric because
\[
(WW^T)^T=WW^T.
\]
It is idempotent because
\[
(WW^T)(WW^T)=W(W^TW)W^T=W I_q W^T=WW^T.
\]
Symmetry and idempotence are the characteristic algebraic properties of an orthogonal projection matrix.



38.0.3 Question 3
Write the \(n\)th observation’s \(i\)th principal component score (i.e. \(Z_{ni}\)) in terms of the row vector \(x_n\in\mathbb R^D\) and the loading vector \(w_i\).


Answer

The \(i\)th score for observation \(n\) is the \(n\)th entry of \(Z_i=Xw_i\), so
\[
z_{ni}=x_n w_i.
\]
Writing \(x_n=(X_{n1},\ldots,X_{nD})\) and \(w_i=(w_{1i},\ldots,w_{Di})^T\) gives
\[
z_{ni}=\sum_{j=1}^D X_{nj}w_{ji}.
\]
At the variable level,
\[
Z_i=Xw_i=w_{1i}X_1+w_{2i}X_2+\cdots+w_{Di}X_D.
\]
Thus each principal component score variable is a linear combination of the original columns of \(X\).



38.0.4 Question 4
Why does the PCA optimization constrain \(\|w\|_2=1\)? Show that without this constraint \[
\operatorname{Var}(Xw)
\] can be made arbitrarily large. (Hint: consider \(w=c w_0\) for a unit vector \(w_0\) and real number \(c\).)


Answer

For centered data,
\[
\operatorname{Var}(Xw)=w^T S_X w.
\]
If \(w\) has positive projected variance, then for any scalar \(c\),
\[
\operatorname{Var}(X(cw))=(cw)^T S_X(cw)=c^2 w^T S_Xw.
\]
Letting \(|c|\to\infty\) makes the variance arbitrarily large without changing the direction of \(w\). The unit-length constraint removes this artificial scaling freedom, so the optimization chooses a direction rather than a vector length.



38.0.5 Question 5
Starting from the sample variance formula for the centered score variable \(z=Xw\), derive
\[
\operatorname{Var}(Xw)=w^T S_X w,
\qquad
S_X=\frac{1}{N-1}X^T X.
\]


Answer

Since \(X\) is centered, \(z=Xw\) is also centered. Its sample variance is
\[
\operatorname{Var}(z)=\frac{1}{N-1}z^Tz.
\]
Substitute \(z=Xw\):
\[
\operatorname{Var}(Xw)
=\frac{1}{N-1}(Xw)^T(Xw)
=\frac{1}{N-1}w^T X^T X w.
\]
Using
\[
S_X=\frac{1}{N-1}X^TX,
\]
we get
\[
\operatorname{Var}(Xw)=w^T S_Xw.
\]



38.0.6 Question 6
For two centered score variables \(Xu\) and \(Xv\), derive a formula for their sample covariance.


Answer

The sample covariance is
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(Xu,Xv)
=\frac{1}{N-1}(Xu)^T(Xv).
\]
Rearranging gives
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(Xu,Xv)
=\frac{1}{N-1}u^T X^T X v
=u^T S_X v.
\]



38.0.7 Question 7
Give noncentered vectors \(x,y\in\mathbb R^3\) with sample covariance zero but raw dot product \(x^Ty\ne 0\).


Answer

Take
\[
x=(1,2,3)^T,
\qquad
y=(2,1,2)^T.
\]
Their means are \(\bar x=2\) and \(\bar y=5/3\), so the centered vectors are
\[
x-\bar x\mathbf 1=(-1,0,1)^T,
\]
and
\[
y-\bar y\mathbf 1=(1/3,-2/3,1/3)^T.
\]
Their centered dot product is
\[
(-1)(1/3)+0(-2/3)+1(1/3)=0,
\]
so their sample covariance is zero. But the raw dot product is
\[
x^Ty=1\cdot2+2\cdot1+3\cdot2=10\ne0.
\]
So uncorrelated means orthogonal only after centering.



38.0.8 Question 8
Use the covariance formula to prove that every eigenvalue of \(S_X\) is nonnegative.


Answer

Let \(v\ne0\) be an eigenvector of \(S_X\) with eigenvalue \(\lambda\). Then
\[
S_Xv=\lambda v.
\]
Multiplying by \(v^T\) gives
\[
v^T S_X v=\lambda v^Tv=\lambda\|v\|_2^2.
\]
But
\[
v^T S_Xv=\operatorname{Var}(Xv)\ge0.
\]
Since \(\|v\|_2^2>0\), it follows that
\[
\lambda\ge0.
\]



38.0.9 Question 9
Complete the main algebra in the simplified Rayleigh quotient theorem: if \(A\) is symmetric with orthonormal eigenvectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_D\) and \(w=\sum_i c_i v_i\), derive the formulas for \(\|w\|_2^2\) and \(w^TAw\) used in the proof.


Answer

Because the eigenvectors are orthonormal,
\[
\|w\|_2^2=w^Tw
=\left(\sum_i c_i v_i\right)^T\left(\sum_j c_j v_j\right)
=\sum_i\sum_j c_i c_j v_i^T v_j
=\sum_i c_i^2.
\]
Also, \(Av_i=\lambda_i v_i\), so
\[
Aw=\sum_i c_i\lambda_i v_i.
\]
Therefore
\[
w^TAw
=\left(\sum_i c_i v_i\right)^T\left(\sum_j c_j\lambda_j v_j\right)
=\sum_i\lambda_i c_i^2.
\]
If \(\|w\|_2=1\), then \(\sum_i c_i^2=1\), so \(w^TAw\) is a weighted average of the eigenvalues with weights \(c_i^2\).



38.0.10 Question 10
In the restricted Rayleigh quotient theorem, \(w\) must satisfy \(w\perp v_1,\ldots,v_{k-1}\). Translate this condition into restrictions on the coefficients \(c_i\) in \(w=\sum_i c_i v_i\), and explain why the maximum value is \(\lambda_k\).


Answer

Since the eigenvectors are orthonormal,
\[
w\perp v_j
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
w^T v_j=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
c_j=0.
\]
Thus the constraints imply
\[
c_1=\cdots=c_{k-1}=0.
\]
For a unit vector satisfying these restrictions,
\[
w^TAw=\lambda_k c_k^2+\lambda_{k+1}c_{k+1}^2+\cdots+\lambda_Dc_D^2.
\]
The remaining weights sum to one, and the largest remaining eigenvalue is \(\lambda_k\). Therefore
\[
w^TAw\le \lambda_k,
\]
with equality when \(c_k=1\) and all other remaining coefficients are zero, i.e. \(w=v_k\) up to sign.



38.0.11 Question 11
The lecture turns the condition \(\operatorname{Cov}(Xw,Xw_1)=0\) into \(w\perp v_1\). How?


Answer

Since \(w_1=v_1\) and \(S_Xv_1=\lambda_1v_1\),
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(Xw,Xw_1)=w^T S_X v_1
=w^T(\lambda_1v_1)
=\lambda_1 w^Tv_1.
\]
If \(\lambda_1>0\), this covariance is zero exactly when
\[
w^Tv_1=0.
\]



38.0.12 Question 12
Derive the covariance matrix of the first \(q\) PCA scores and show why it is diagonal when \(W_q=[v_1\;v_2\;\cdots\;v_q]\).


Answer

The score matrix is
\[
Z_q=XW_q.
\]
Because \(X\) is centered, the sample covariance matrix of the scores is
\[
S_{Z_q}=\frac{1}{N-1}Z_q^T Z_q.
\]
Substitute \(Z_q=XW_q\):
\[
S_{Z_q}
=\frac{1}{N-1}W_q^T X^TX W_q
=W_q^T S_X W_q.
\]
The \((i,j)\) entry is
\[
v_i^T S_X v_j=v_i^T(\lambda_j v_j)=\lambda_j v_i^T v_j.
\]
This equals \(\lambda_i\) when \(i=j\) and \(0\) when \(i\ne j\). Therefore
\[
S_{Z_q}=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_q).
\]



38.0.13 Question 13
Check the lecture’s claim that the PCA score variables are centered whenever the columns of \(X\) are centered.


Answer

Let \(\mathbf 1\in\mathbb R^N\) be the vector of all ones. The columns of \(X\) are centered exactly when
\[
\mathbf 1^T X=0^T.
\]
For \(Z_q=XW_q\),
\[
\mathbf 1^T Z_q
=\mathbf 1^T XW_q
=(\mathbf 1^T X)W_q
=0^T W_q
=0^T.
\]
So every column of \(Z_q\) has sample mean zero.



38.0.14 Question 14
Take the lecture’s definition of total variance across the original centered variables and prove
\[
\sum_{j=1}^D \widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(X_j)=\operatorname{tr}(S_X)=\sum_{j=1}^D\lambda_j.
\]


Answer

The diagonal entries of \(S_X\) are the sample variances of the original variables:
\[
(S_X)_{jj}=\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(X_j).
\]
Therefore
\[
\sum_{j=1}^D \widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(X_j)=\sum_{j=1}^D (S_X)_{jj}=\operatorname{tr}(S_X).
\]
For any square matrix, the trace equals the sum of its eigenvalues.
\[
\operatorname{tr}(S_X)=\sum_{j=1}^D\lambda_j.
\]



38.0.15 Question 15
Using the centered data matrix with rows \((1,0)\), \((-1,0)\), \((0,2)\), and \((0,-2)\), compute \(S_X\), the two PCA directions, their eigenvalues, and the proportion of variance captured by the first PC.


Answer

Here \(N=4\) and
\[
X^TX=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&8\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Thus
\[
S_X=\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&8\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}2/3&0\\0&8/3\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The largest eigenvalue is
\[
\lambda_1=8/3
\]
with direction \(v_1=(0,1)^T\) up to sign. The second eigenvalue is
\[
\lambda_2=2/3
\]
with direction \(v_2=(1,0)^T\) up to sign.
The first PC captures
\[
\frac{8/3}{8/3+2/3}=\frac{8}{10}=0.8
\]
of the total variance.



38.0.16 Question 16
A covariance matrix has tied eigenvalues, for example
\[
S=\operatorname{diag}(2,2,1).
\]
Describe exactly what is nonunique about the PCA directions. What remains well-defined if \(q=2\)?


Answer

The first two eigenvalues are tied, so every unit vector in
\[
\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2)
\]
is a leading eigenvector with eigenvalue \(2\). If \(q=1\), the first PC direction is not unique: any line through the origin inside that two-dimensional eigenspace is optimal.
If \(q=2\), the individual basis vectors are still not unique, because any orthonormal basis of \(\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2)\) works. However, the two-dimensional subspace itself is well-defined, so the projection onto that subspace is unique.



38.0.17 Question 17
Changing a loading vector from \(v_i\) to \(-v_i\) is allowed in PCA. State what happens to the score \(z_i=Xv_i\) and its variance.


Answer

If \(v_i\) is replaced by \(-v_i\), then the score becomes
\[
X(-v_i)=-Xv_i=-z_i.
\]
The variance is unchanged because
\[
\operatorname{Var}(-z_i)=\operatorname{Var}(z_i).
\]
Thus the sign of a loading vector is arbitrary. Only relative signs within a loading vector have interpretive meaning after a sign convention has been chosen.



38.0.18 Question 18
If every column has been centered and scaled to sample variance \(1\), what are the diagonal entries and trace of \(S_X\)? Why does this matter when variables use different units?


Answer

After sample standardization, each variable has sample variance \(1\), so
\[
(S_X)_{jj}=1
\]
for every \(j\). The covariance matrix is then the sample correlation matrix, and
\[
\operatorname{tr}(S_X)=D.
\]
This matters because variables measured in large numerical units can otherwise dominate the covariance matrix simply due to scale. Standardizing puts all variables on a common variance scale before PCA chooses high-variance directions.

title: 39  K-means - Review Questions
text:
